extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political history and constitutional theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess institutional features, norms, and effects of ancient Greek and Roman governments (monarchies, aristocracies, democracies) as described in historical/political narrative. Emphasizes what constitutional arrangements promoted balance, stability, or public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial authority exercised in national assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial authority was commonly exercised in national assemblies — 'Licet apud concilium accufare quoque, et difcrimen capitis intendere...' (Latin passage describing punishments, suspensions, and public executions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats judicial functions handled publicly by assemblies as a defining institutional practice; when evaluating an ancient constitution, note whether major criminal/penal decisions and differentiations of punishment were processed in popular or national councils rather than by separate judicial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitution (monarchy + aristocracy + democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixture of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy is visible in many Greek states (kings among archons, councils of princes, assemblies of the people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the government by identifying the presence and relative strength of the three orders (king/monarchic element, noble/senatorial aristocracy, popular assemblies). The balance among these orders determines whether a state functions as a monarchy, aristocracy, or republic in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the people: limited religious/judicial functions versus regular civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The people's authority often appears 'as judges of certain religious ceremonies' rather than as any regular civil authority; their role was sometimes limited to ritual or confirmatory acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish formal participatory roles (e.g., ceremonial/judicial-religious) from substantive civil powers. A constitution that confines popular power to religious or symbolic acts grants little real check on elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch as 'first among equals' (limited royal preeminence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The king often appears 'little more among the archons than the first among equals' — monarch with precedence but not absolute authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing monarchical systems, consider whether the monarch is merely a primus inter pares with limited prerogatives or holds unilateral/legislative power; the distinction affects constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular assemblies frequent but constitutionally weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular assemblies were frequent and freedom of speech in them advanced, yet demagogues had 'very little influence' and 'popular assemblies had as yet very little constitutional power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure not only the frequency of assemblies or freedom of speech, but their actual constitutional power (ability to make binding decisions, initiate legislation, or check elites). Applause for a leader and suppression of dissent are signs of limited popular power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for written laws and defined prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The continual fluctuations of law and uncertainty of life, liberty, and property arose from 'the want of having the prerogatives and privileges of those orders defined' and 'no laws were written.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A durable constitution requires clearly defined prerogatives and written laws; absence of written law and undefined privileges leads to instability and frequent revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession rules and primogeniture shaped by religion/opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of primogeniture was favoured by popular opinion because kings claimed descent from Jupiter; succession was shaped by religious ideas as much as legal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate succession mechanisms (primogeniture, competitive succession, elective elements) and the extent to which religious legitimacy or popular sentiment, rather than codified law, governs succession—this affects predictability of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of ruler relative to nobles affects institutional balance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prince was brave and able he 'governed as he pleased'; when feeble, archons grew ambitious and limited royal power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how personal capacity of rulers interacts with institutional checks: weak rulers invite aristocratic encroachment; strong rulers can dominate when checks are ineffective. Robust constitutional design should not depend on ruler character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative origin and aristocratic negative (Spartan senate)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sparta all laws 'were to originate' in the senate of twenty-eight, which had a negative before debate; the senate held most executive and important legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze where legislation originates and which body holds veto/negative powers. Concentration of legislative initiation and veto in a hereditary oligarchy points to oligarchic dominance rather than popular rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular assemblies limited to yes/no ratification (no debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lycurgus entrusted assemblies only with 'the power of confirming or rejecting what the senate proposed, and expressly forbade them all debate' — citizens gave 'simple ayes or noes' without being allowed to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of citizen participation: passive referendum-style ratification versus active deliberative debate radically changes the democratic content of assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive oversight magistrates (the ephors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five magistrates (the ephori) were instituted 'to inspect the administration, and maintain the constitution; to convoke, prorogue, and dissolve' assemblies; they were annually appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess existence and powers of oversight bodies tasked with inspecting administration and enforcing constitutional norms. Annual appointment and specific powers (convoking/dissolving assemblies) are important features to note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal oaths and religious opinion as constitutional balancing mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath taken every month by kings and ephori was ordered: kings swore to observe the laws; ephori swore to maintain hereditary honours and revere the kings as ministers of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize reliance on oaths, religion, and public opinion to sustain balance where legal/negative checks are absent. Such mechanisms may enforce order but are weaker than independent legal vetoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of assemblies (city vs country) to avoid jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous separation of the city from the country into two assemblies 'avoided the danger of jealousies between town and country' and 'doubled the chances' for preserving monarchical and democratic importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying institutional design, note geographic/constituency separation of assemblies as a mechanism to balance competing interests (town vs country) and provide multiple checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance requires an independent negative in each branch
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempted balance in Sparta 'was not equivalent to a negative in each' branch; absence of a negative rendered the balance incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A durable balance of powers typically requires some form of independent negative (veto/check) in each branch; mere mutual oaths or opinion-based checks are insufficient to guarantee equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies that undermine general welfare (property equalization, bans, exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures such as 'equal division of property; the banishment of gold and silver; prohibition of travel... prohibition of arts, trades, and agriculture; discouragement of literature; public meals; exposure of weak children' served family pride and state spectacle but harmed happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether constitutional/social policies promote overall public welfare and liberty or primarily serve elite/familial prestige. Draconian social engineering that sacrifices comforts, arts, and natural population growth is critiqued as inimical to happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population as an indicator of national happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Population, 'the surest indication of national happiness,' decreased under Spartan laws; demographic decline signals constitutional failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic health (population stability/growth) as one metric for assessing whether institutions promote the common welfare and family flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between appearance of political liberty and substantive civil liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'the people's consent was necessary to every law' (appearance of political liberty), the civil liberty was 'little better than that of a man chained in a dungeon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish formal procedures (consent requirements, assemblies) from actual civil liberties (freedom to speak, act, own property). A constitution can have procedures that mask substantive unfreedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of authority in a single center leads to oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legislature rested wholly in the senate, the constitution 'would have been in effect a simple hereditary oligarchy' with authority nearly collected into one center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for institutional designs that centralize legislative, executive, and judicial powers in one body or social order; this concentration is a marker of oligarchic, not republican, rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of education and public physical exercises to strengthen citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises like running, wrestling, riding, swimming, skating, fencing, dancing 'should be introduced into public and private education... would fortify the bodies and invigorate the minds of youth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider civic education (including physical training) as part of constitutional health. The author endorses incorporating vigorous physical education to produce robust citizens, while criticizing exclusion of letters and arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness (travel, intercourse) versus isolationist prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions on travel and intercourse with strangers and the forbidding of arts/trade were intended to preserve family pride but proved counterproductive (foreign manners intruded and laws were evaded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policies restricting movement and exchange: isolationist prohibitions may be ineffective and undermine prosperity; openness tends to introduce new manners and commerce that affect stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of royal functions (religion, war, not legislation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings were to 'confirm high priests; to be commanders in chief of the armies, and presidents of the senate' but 'legislation was never within their prerogative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping institutional roles, note whether the monarch has religious and military primacy but is explicitly excluded from legislative initiative—this shapes the monarch's actual power and limits.
